assessment.nobel_worthiness: Very high. This body of work brought constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal institutions into formal economic analysis, linking theory to empirical tests. It changed how economists explain why policies and growth outcomes differ across states, and it connects well to the long-run historical literature on institutions and state building.
assessment.attribution: The Persson-Tabellini collaboration is the core of the field, with a widely used synthesis in the political economics volumes. Besley's work on state capacity and accountability is a strong complementary strand. A three-person prize is coherent, though other contributors to the political economy literature could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The central contributions date from the 1990s and 2000s and have been replicated, extended and absorbed into mainstream economics and political science for decades.
uncertainties: The Committee has already recognised institutions-and-growth work, which may affect perceived novelty.
The boundary with the political science literature may complicate how credit is divided.
My knowledge of the latest developments in the field is incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Very high. Collateral constraints and credit-cycle amplification explain how small shocks become large and persistent downturns. Kiyotaki-Moore and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator became the foundation for macro-financial modelling and for the post-2008 policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 credit cycles paper is the clear theoretical origin. Gertler is central through the financial accelerator and later macro-financial models. Gilchrist is an important co-author, and Bernanke's earlier Nobel recognised related work, so a three-person prize is defensible but leaves out some contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The ideas are about thirty years old and the framework is embedded in central bank models and the financial crisis literature.
uncertainties: Part of the intellectual territory overlaps with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Attribution relative to Bernanke and Gilchrist is debatable.
Gertler also appears in the broader New Keynesian candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. Linking population-scale administrative records to measure intergenerational mobility and neighbourhood effects created new facts and a new empirical standard. It has had a major effect on public policy debate and on the study of inequality of opportunity. The data-building approach is similar to historical dataset construction.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader of the programme. Hendren and Friedman are central co-authors on place effects and the mobility atlas work. Katz's earlier Moving to Opportunity work is also credited on the longlist, so the line of credit is somewhat diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Moderate to high. The main papers are from roughly 2014 onward, and the findings have been extended and debated, but the long-term durability of some causal claims is still being tested.
uncertainties: The programme is relatively young for a prize.
Chetty appears in other candidate groupings, which complicates attribution.
Some causal interpretations of place effects remain debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. The task-based approach and the China-shock evidence changed understanding of how technology and trade reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality. The work is strongly empirical and relevant to the distributional effects of technological change.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the trade-shock work. Dorn and Hanson are co-authors on the China shock papers. Acemoglu and others contributed to the task-based theory but are not credited here, so this credit allocation is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Moderate to high. The key papers date from the early 2000s through 2013, and the findings have been tested, replicated and refined in many countries.
uncertainties: The recent prize for innovation and growth may reduce the near-term appetite for adjacent technology topics.
The persistence and size of the trade-shock effects have been debated.
The task-based theory is only partly covered by the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. Nominal rigidities, staggered pricing and the policy-rule perspective gave the foundation of the framework used by central banks. The New Keynesian approach shaped both the theory and practice of monetary policy.
assessment.attribution: Calvo's pricing model, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's integrated synthesis are distinct and identifiable contributions. The longlist includes eight names, which shows how diffuse credit is, and others such as Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler also have strong claims.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. Core contributions date from the 1980s to the early 2000s and have been in policy use for decades.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse, and any three-person selection excludes strong contributors.
Post-2008 critiques of the framework may affect its standing.
The Committee has recognised the rational expectations and monetary policy tradition several times already.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High on data and impact. Building long-run top-income series from tax records, and later estimates of wealth and offshore holdings, transformed the measurement of inequality and shaped the debate about it. This is close to the historical national accounts tradition and is a major data contribution.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the origin of the top-income series, and Zucman is central to wealth and offshore wealth estimation. The world inequality database is a collective effort with many other contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature on the top-income series, which date from the early 2000s, but less settled on wealth and offshore estimates.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes about wealth and top-income estimates, especially assumptions in distributional accounts, remain unresolved.
The policy advocacy of some laureates could influence perceptions.
The contribution is mainly measurement and empirical rather than theoretical.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. Formal models of fairness and reciprocity, together with experimental evidence on strong reciprocity and punishment, changed how economists model motivation, contracts and cooperation. This brought behavioural insights into mainstream theory in a testable way.
assessment.attribution: The Fehr-Schmidt inequity aversion model is the clearest formal contribution, and Fehr's experimental programme is the empirical core. Falk has important work on fairness and its field relevance, but I prefer a narrower two-person prize on the central model and evidence. Bolton and Ockenfels also developed a closely related model, which is not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key papers are from about 1999 onward and have been widely replicated and applied.
uncertainties: Some replication and external validity questions for lab-based social preferences remain.
Behavioural economics has been recognised several times, which may reduce priority.
The omission of Bolton and Ockenfels and of other behavioural contributors complicates attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Moderately high. Methods that test for and quantify adverse selection and moral hazard in real insurance markets connect classic information economics with welfare measurement and policy design in health insurance. The empirical work established credible approaches to quantifying selection costs.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the leading figures for welfare estimation and empirical design in insurance markets. Salanie contributed to the early empirical test of asymmetric information. The theoretical foundations were already recognised in the 2001 prize.
assessment.maturity: Moderate. The main papers are from the 2000s and 2010s and have been extended, but the long-term effect is still developing.
uncertainties: The contribution is mostly applied and methodological on top of previously recognised theory.
Relative standing against other strong empirical candidates is uncertain.
Distinguishing the contributions of Finkelstein and Einav from those of other co-authors in the health economics literature is difficult.
